c.tagline: Ancient souqs, olive-oil soap, and the sweetest kanafeh in the Middle East

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'service' taxis run fixed routes for a small flat fare; private taxis should agree on a price or confirm the meter before riding.

emergency.note: The Palestine Red Crescent Society runs ambulance service (101); police and medical response times can be affected by checkpoints and access restrictions.

avoid.reason: Stay clear of Balata and Askar refugee camps and any checkpoint or area with active unrest — military raids and clashes can erupt with little warning, so check the news daily.
Avoid demonstrations and after-dark movement, and be ready for sudden checkpoint closures on roads in and out of the city.

hood_desc: The heart of Nablus, a dense Ottoman-era souq of stone alleys, soap factories, spice stalls, and kanafeh shops that has been continuously inhabited for centuries. Landmarks like the Great Mosque and several 18th-century hammams sit alongside working soap workshops.
A leafier, more modern district west of downtown, home to An-Najah National University and many of the city's newer cafes, shops, and apartment buildings favored by students and professionals.
Named for its natural springs, this older neighborhood on the western edge of the Old City has traditional stone houses and quieter streets, with views up toward Mount Gerizim.

The mountain overlooking the city from the south, home to a small Samaritan community at Kiryat Luza and ancient ruins including a ruined Byzantine church; reachable by road with sweeping views over Nablus.
The commercial center of the newer city, anchored by Al-Manara clock tower square, with banks, shops, and the busiest streets for everyday city life outside the Old City.

water.note: Supply and quality vary; most visitors stick to bottled water.

transit.map: no official app; ask locally or hotel staff for routes
transit.note: There is no fixed public transit map; shared 'service' taxis are the main way to get around and between towns.

air: No airport; nearest is Ben Gurion Airport (TLV) in Israel
train: No rail service in the West Bank
bus: Regular service taxis and buses connect Nablus to Ramallah, Jenin, and other West Bank cities

airport.name: Ben Gurion Airport (TLV)
rentals: Not available locally; arranged via Israeli airport agencies

tip.r: Tipping is not customary; rounding up a bill or leaving small change for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Knafeh Nabulsieh
food.desc: The original: soft white nabulsi cheese under orange-tinted shredded pastry, baked in huge trays, drenched in rose syrup and scattered with pistachio.

places.name: Al-Aqsa Sweets
places.note: Sixty-year-old knafeh-only bakery turning out dozens of trays a day; no colouring, no shortcuts.

places.name: Al-Aker Sweets
places.note: Nablus-founded sweet house whose knafeh made the city's name across the region.

places.name: Halawiyat Dimashq
places.note: Always crowded; locals say the queue is part of the experience.

food.name: Musakhan
food.desc: Palestine's national dish: roast chicken over taboon bread soaked in local olive oil, piled with sumac-stained onions and toasted pine nuts.

places.name: Beit al-Karama
places.note: Women-run kitchen and cooking school serving Nabulsi home cooking to order.

places.name: Zeit ou Zaatar
places.note: Popular modern Palestinian restaurant built around olive oil, za'atar and taboon bread.

places.name: Khan al-Tujjar taboon bakeries
places.note: Wood-fired taboon ovens in the old market where the bread itself is the point.

food.name: Hummus and fatteh breakfast
food.desc: Warm hummus swirled with olive oil and whole chickpeas, or layered fatteh with yoghurt and pine nuts; eaten early with pickles and raw onion.

places.name: Sahat al-Manara hummus counters
places.note: Morning-only hummus shops around the clock square; sold out by mid-morning.

places.name: Zeit ou Zaatar
places.note: Sit-down breakfast plates for visitors who miss the early market rush.

places.name: Al-Nasr Street falafel stands
places.note: Falafel fried to order and stuffed into bread with hummus and salad.

food.name: Tamriyeh
food.desc: A Nablus-only pastry: semolina custard folded into thin dough, deep-fried in ghee and dusted heavily with icing sugar. Eaten hot, standing up.

places.name: Old City tamriyeh stands
places.note: Fried to order in shallow ghee pans; a Nablus speciality you rarely find elsewhere.

places.name: Al-Aqsa Sweets area sweet shops
places.note: Cluster of old-city sweet makers where tamriyeh appears beside the knafeh trays.

food.name: Maqluba
food.desc: The 'upside-down' pot: rice layered with fried aubergine, cauliflower and lamb or chicken, then flipped onto a tray and served with cool yoghurt.

places.name: Beit al-Karama
places.note: Cooked as a family would make it; best arranged in advance.

places.name: Zeit ou Zaatar
places.note: Dependable place to find the classic Palestinian rice dishes on a set menu.

food.name: Nabulsi olive oil, za'atar and makdous
food.desc: The mezze that defines the hills around Nablus: green new-press olive oil, wild za'atar, salty nabulsi cheese and walnut-stuffed pickled aubergine.

places.name: Khan al-Tujjar souq
places.note: Historic merchants' market for oil, za'atar, olives, cheese and makdous by weight.

places.name: Souq al-Basal
places.note: Produce market where the autumn olive pressing is sold straight from the mills.

places.name: Zeit ou Zaatar
places.note: Restaurant named for the pairing; good place to taste it laid out as breakfast.

food.name: Tamr hindi and sous
food.desc: Street coolers of tamarind and bitter licorice poured from ornate brass urns by roving vendors who clink brass cups to advertise themselves.

places.name: Sahat al-Manara vendors
places.note: Brass-urn sellers work the clock square and the souq entrances all afternoon.

places.name: Khan al-Tujjar souq
places.note: Cold tamarind and carob drinks sold along the covered market lanes.

food.name: Cardamom coffee and sahlab
food.desc: Dark Arabic coffee ground with green cardamom, or in winter sahlab, a hot milk pudding-drink dusted with cinnamon, coconut and crushed pistachio.

places.name: Old City coffee roasters
places.note: Beans roasted and ground with cardamom while you wait; strong take-away cups.

places.name: Al-Aker Sweets
places.note: Sweet house where a coffee alongside the knafeh is the standard order.

landmarks: Old City of Nablus
A living Ottoman-era warren of vaulted souqs, spice stalls, and stone khans where the scent of fresh knafeh drifts through centuries-old alleys.
Jacob's Well
Within a Greek Orthodox church at Balata lies the deep well where tradition says Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman, venerated for two millennia.
Mount Gerizim
Sacred summit of the world's last Samaritan community, whose hilltop village, ancient ruins, and Passover traditions overlook all of Nablus.
Tell Balata (Ancient Shechem)
Bronze Age ramparts and a massive temple mound mark biblical Shechem, one of the oldest continuously storied sites in the Holy Land.
An-Nasr Mosque
The silver-domed 'Mosque of Victory' rises at the old city's heart on foundations that served Byzantine and Crusader churches before it.
Great Mosque of Nablus
Converted from a Crusader-Byzantine basilica, the city's largest historic mosque stretches its long colonnaded hall along the main Roman axis.
Traditional Soap Factories
Centuries-old saboun nabulsi workshops still stack towers of olive-oil soap cubes by hand, a fragrant emblem of the city's craft heritage.
Hammam al-Shifa
A restored Ottoman bathhouse from 1624 still steams in the old city, offering marble slabs, massages, and mint tea under pierced domes.
Sebastia (Samaria)
Roman colonnades, a theatre, and the traditional tomb of John the Baptist crown this hilltop village of ancient Samaria north of Nablus.
Knafeh Quarter and Al-Qasaba Street
The bustling commercial spine of the old city is the birthplace of knafeh nabulsiyeh, where copper trays of the syrupy cheese pastry emerge nonstop.

train.note: There is no rail service in the West Bank. The Ottoman Hejaz Railway branch that once ran down the Jezreel Valley towards Nablus was abandoned decades ago and none of it carries passengers today. Israel Railways' network stops well outside the West Bank and is not a practical part of a journey to Nablus, so everything comes in by road.

bus.note: Buses and servees taxis use the main bus station in the city centre, a short walk from the Old City and the casbah. From Jerusalem the usual route is the #18 Arab bus from the Sultan Suleiman Street station to Ramallah for about 7 shekels, then a Nablus bus for around 10.5 shekels or a servees for about 17, taking roughly an hour. Direct servees also link Nablus with Jenin, Tulkarm and Jericho, all paid in cash with no timetable - vehicles leave when full. There is no international coach: Jordan is reached via Jericho and the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge with a Jordanian visa arranged in advance, and checkpoint closures around Nablus can add hours to any of this.

ferry.note: Nablus lies inland in the hills between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, with no coastline or navigable water anywhere near it, so no ferry service exists.

half.name: Ramallah
half.blurb: The de facto Palestinian administrative center, with a lively downtown, cafes, and the Yasser Arafat Museum.

half.name: Jericho
half.blurb: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, near the Mount of Temptation cable car and the Dead Sea lowlands.

half.name: Hebron
half.blurb: An ancient city centered on the Ibrahimi Mosque and Cave of the Patriarchs, a site sacred to Judaism and Islam.
